thesis: This episode argues that Trader Joe's is a unique, culturally relevant outlier in the essential grocery category with significant international expansion potential. It contrasts Trader Joe's low-SKU, high-turnover model with competitors like Costco, Walmart, and Kroger to highlight its distinct operational efficiency and margin focus.

claims.claim: The speakers mention a connection between Trader Joe's and Nvidia via coworkers, specifically that Jensen Huang was a coworker at Trader Joe's.
claims.quote: David: Yes, me too. But there is a direct connection between Trader Joe's and Nvidia via coworkers. Ben: You heard it here first. Trader Joe and Jensen Huang were coworkers at one point in time.

claims.claim: David states a preference for Meta glasses over AirPods, noting he doesn't like having things in his ears.
claims.quote: David: I can second that. I got them, too. By far the best AirPods yet. I still prefer the Meta glasses, though. I've just realized I really don't like having things in my ears.

claims.claim: Ben suggests that an episode on Amazon Part 1 may be of interest, describing Trader Joe's as the anti-Amazon.
claims.quote: Ben: Absolutely. Walmart. Perhaps Amazon Part 1 also may be of interest, since this is effectively the anti-Amazon: it's the everything store and the very few things store.

claims.claim: David mentions that the show made an episode on Whole Foods back in the day, noting the day Amazon bought the company.
claims.quote: David: Oh, and Ben, how could we forget? We made an episode on Whole Foods back in the day. Ben: We did. David: The day that Amazon bought the company.

claims.claim: Costco is used as a similar business comparison, growing about 8% per year with a 3% net income margin and trading at 1.6x revenue.
claims.quote: So first, let's look at Costco, the most similar business in some ways. Costco is growing about 8% per year, so probably a little slower than Trader Joe's by most estimates, and has a 3% net income margin. Costco trades at 1.6x revenue, sky high.

claims.claim: Walmart is compared as a second comp with similar net income margins and growth, trading at 1.3x revenue.
claims.quote: Walmart, which isn't all grocery, but a lot of it is grocery, has similar net income margins, similar growth. Maybe it grows a little slower than Costco. Walmart trades at 1.3x revenue.

claims.claim: Kroger trades at 0.3x revenue and is described as a slower growth business with razor-thin net income margins between 1 and 2%.
claims.quote: Kroger trades at 0.3x revenue and Albertsons at 0.1x revenue. Those are much slower growth businesses. And Kroger is actually shrinking with razor-thin net income margins between 1 and 2%.

claims.claim: Albertsons trades at 0.1x revenue and is described as a much slower growth business.
claims.quote: Kroger trades at 0.3x revenue and Albertsons at 0.1x revenue. Those are much slower growth businesses.

claims.claim: Trader Joe's is viewed as an outlier and a much smaller business than usually covered, with nearly infinite expansion potential internationally.
claims.quote: Unacquired. I think that's actually the wrong takeaway. Yeah, Trader Joe's, first Joe, and now under the ownership of the Albrecht Foundations, is willing to play such a long game. In the fullness of time, I bet Trader Joe's will be worth at least 10x that.

claims.claim: Trader Joe's is culturally relevant in an essential category and has built one of the most culturally relevant brands in an essential category.
claims.quote: And Trader Joe's happens to have built one of the most, or probably the most, culturally relevant brand in an essential category, even if it ends up financially not being as valuable as these other companies we cover.

claims.claim: Trader Joe's merchandise everything like wines and need to be a merchant and have an assortment rather than stock everything.
claims.quote: You should always remember that Trader Joe's started as a wine merchant, and they merchandise everything like wines. And that's exactly how you would behave as a wine merchant. There's no way you could ever stock every wine in the world. You need to be a merchant and have an assortment.

claims.claim: Trader Joe's focuses on the absolute dollars of margin in each item rather than the margin percentage of each item.
claims.quote: A corollary to that: they aren't focused on the margin percentage of each item. We didn't talk about this yet, but they actually don't apply a consistent markup. They focus on the absolute dollars of margin in each item.

claims.claim: Trader Joe's has a low SKU count of about 4,000 SKUs and keeps this constraint aggressively to not waste money on less productive square feet.
claims.quote: Okay, so they've got this low SKU count. Not as low as the old days, but still only like 4,000 SKUs. And if you keep this constraint really aggressively, it means that you're not wasting money on your less productive square feet.

claims.claim: Trader Joe's turns over their inventory 60 times per year and sells through everything in the store.
claims.quote: I mean, I saw one stat that they turn over their inventory 60 times per year, which is more than once a week. They sell through everything in the store.

claims.claim: Costco is a much bigger business than Trader Joe's with 10x revenue, but margins are lower with 11-14% markups.
claims.quote: By the way, we should say for anyone who's wondering, Costco is a much, much, much bigger business than Trader Joe's. They're sort of cousins of each other in business model, different in all the ways we've talked about. But Costco's revenue is 10x—maybe more. Last year, it was $275 billion. Now, margins are a different story. They famously only mark up 11 to 14%

claims.claim: Costco is a successful public company that is cut from the same cloth as Trader Joe's.
claims.quote: David: Yeah, the one store that's out there that is cut from the same cloth as us, is Costco.
